papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.title: Dollo Parsimony Overestimates Ancestral Gene Content Reconstructions
papers.authors: Gàlvez-Morante A, Guéguen L, Natsidis P, Telford MJ, Richter DJ
papers.question: Does Dollo parsimony give accurate ancestral gene counts?
papers.tried: Compare reconstructed ancestral gene totals with the truth in simulations.
papers.method_data: Simulated gene content with a known ancestor; Dollo parsimony and other counting methods.
papers.key_results: Dollo parsimony overestimates ancestral gene content. Accuracy is judged on totals per node, not on individual families.
papers.limits: Does not test reconciliation methods such as ALE, and does not check calibration of per-family probabilities.
papers.ideas_for_us: Closest known-truth test of ancestral gene content. Ours differs: it scores ALE root posteriors family by family, with a reliability curve and ECE.

papers.title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world
papers.authors: Hauf S, Baidya L, Nakamura R, Fine JL, Guyen HT, Moses A, Dindo M
papers.question: Can a compartment built from nucleotides themselves, with no polymer, protect RNA and reshape its chemistry in a way that helps the RNA world?
papers.tried: Liquid condensates of nucleotides (such as ATP) with divalent cations and a short alcohol or diol act as the first compartment, before membranes.
papers.method_data: Condensate formation from nucleotides, divalent cations and short-chain alcohols or diols in water; RNA and DNA uptake; RNA and a phosphate-ester model substrate under acid; hammerhead ribozyme at neutral pH; coarse-grained simulations; phospholipid organisation at the droplet surface.
papers.key_results: (abstract only) Condensates form spontaneously without any polymer and concentrate RNA and DNA. RNA survives for days inside them under acidic conditions that rapidly hydrolyse it in bulk; a phosphate-ester model substrate shows the same, which the authors read as suppressed backbone cleavage. Simulations suggest magnesium-phosphate bridging and a strongly water-depleted interior. At neutral pH the hammerhead ribozyme shifts from cleavage toward religation. Droplets organise phospholipids at their surface.
papers.limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Abstract only: the full text returned a bot block (403), so no rates, concentrations or alcohol levels were seen. Needs millimolar-scale nucleotides plus an alcohol or diol; whether such conditions are plausible on early Earth is not shown in the abstract.
papers.ideas_for_us: In the step tables (B3), add a nucleotide-condensate option to the compartment step and to the RNA-hydrolysis hand-off of the pond route, scored as 'preprint, one lab' until replicated. Record what nucleotide and diol concentrations it needs once the full text is readable, and check them against the phosphate and nucleotide supply rows.

papers.title: Transport dynamics across prebiotic hydrothermal mineral barriers: comparison with contemporary proton motive pathways
papers.authors: Altair T, Lindenfelser E, Galante D, Varela H, De Decker Y, Hudson R
papers.question: Do vent-type iron minerals conduct ions as well as electrons, so that charge can stay balanced while electrons cross a mineral wall to reduce CO2?
papers.tried: Electron transfer across vent walls may be fast, but each electron needs a matching ion; ionic conduction could be the bottleneck.
papers.method_data: FeS, Fe(Ni)S and green rust made by co-precipitation, centrifuged to pastes, hydrated with ocean-analogue fluid (0.108 cm3 between graphite electrodes). Two-electrode impedance spectroscopy at open circuit, 1 Hz-1 MHz, 10 mV, room temperature; equivalent-circuit fits (2-15% parameter error).
papers.key_results: Electronic conductivity 1.5e-2, 1.2e-2 and 6.7e-3 S/cm; ionic 4.97e-7, 2.37e-8 and 8.12e-9 S/cm (FeS, Fe(Ni)S, green rust). Living membranes from the literature: about 5e-10 electronic and 1.27e-8 ionic.
papers.limits: No CO2 reduction measured, no pH gradient applied, pastes are not chimney walls, room temperature only. Short communication.
papers.ideas_for_us: In the vent route step table (#4), split charge balance across the wall from electron transfer and score it as its own step with these conductivities and caveats.
papers.changes_plan: Adds a separate charge-balance step to the vent route table (#4); not a change to the scoring rule.

papers.title: Mafic-ultramafic igneous rocks as a source of reactive phosphorus for the origin of life
papers.authors: Baidya AS, Walton CR, Kalita J, Szilas K, Viccaro M, Savage PS, Allison S, Nisbet EG, et al.
papers.question: Could ordinary early-Earth volcanic rocks (basalt, komatiite, peridotite) have been a steady source of the reactive phosphorus forms phosphite and pyrophosphate, instead of rare meteorite or lightning sources?
papers.tried: Reduced and polymerized phosphorus forms magmatically in hot, iron-rich, low-water rocks, and seafloor or lake weathering of those rocks releases it.
papers.method_data: Phosphorus speciation in rocks and olivine separates from 15 localities, a crustal mass balance for 3.5 to 2.0 Ga oceanic crust, and simple box models for phosphite in the deep ocean and in a Mono Lake-like volcanic lake.
papers.key_results: Phosphite reached up to 7%, 24%, 17% and 0.6% of total P in olivine separates, peridotite, komatiite and basalt; average phosphite shares were 0.22% (basalt), 4.89% (komatiite), 5.33% (olivine) and 5.52% (peridotite). Pyrophosphate reached up to 5% (komatiite) and 0.4% (basalt). Oceanic crust from 3.5 to 2.0 Ga held phosphite and pyrophosphate at 4 to 5 ppm each. The ocean box model gives an upper-bound steady state of up to 1 nM phosphite with surface UV oxidation, rising to 1 to 2 µM if photo-oxidation is suppressed (the abstract quotes up to 1 µM). A UV-shielded lake reaches up to 67 µM; a lake with strong photo-oxidation stays below 0.1 µM. They argue the phosphite and pyrophosphate are magmatic, not from later alteration.
papers.limits: Box models are simple: weathering is the only source, adsorption onto clays is assumed minor, and no model was possible for pyrophosphate. Lake values depend strongly on the assumed phosphite half-life (UV exposure). Rock samples are modern exposures, not Hadean crust. The paper does not test whether these concentrations are enough to phosphorylate anything.
papers.ideas_for_us: Add a crustal phosphite supply row to the vent and pond step tables (#4/#5/#20) with the paper's numbers: about 1 nM in an open ocean, 1 to 2 µM under suppressed photo-oxidation, up to 67 µM in a UV-shielded lake, below 0.1 µM in an exposed lake. Then check, with our hashed compatibility rule, whether any downstream phosphorylation step's required concentration is met without purification. Pair with Gull et al. 2026 (phosphite oxidation coupled to adenosine phosphorylation) to build a two-step phosphite route in the pond map.
papers.changes_plan: The pathway map's phosphorus supply step for the pond and vent routes can now be scored with measured rock phosphite shares and modeled concentrations (up to 67 µM in a UV-shielded lake) instead of meteoritic phosphide only. This is a step-table update, not a change to the scoring rule.

papers.title: Breaking Kinetic Symmetry: How Wet-Dry Cycling Ratchets Prebiotic Chemistry Far from Equilibrium
papers.authors: Capera-Aragones P, Rajaei V, Deans-Rowe A, DiGiacomo J, Smith DE, Frenkel-Pinter M, Williams LD
papers.question: Why does wet-dry cycling accumulate condensation products instead of just oscillating around equilibrium?
papers.tried: Kinetic modeling of condensation, hydrolysis and exchange among mercapto acids, hydroxy acids and amino acids.
papers.method_data: Kinetic model.
papers.key_results: A ratchet: second-order exchange is fast when dry and suppressed by dilution when wet, so thioesters and esters convert to amides but not back, driving directional accumulation. No numbers in the abstract.
papers.limits: (abstract only) Model only; rate constants and their sources not read.

papers.title: Concurrent Phosphite Oxidation and Adenosine Phosphorylation Under Prebiotic Evaporative Conditions
papers.authors: Gull M, Šponer JE, Cruz HA, Gallazi EJ, Smith B, McCallum SA, Rogers KL, Pasek MA
papers.question: Can phosphite be oxidised and attached to adenosine at the same time in a warm evaporating pool?
papers.tried: Phosphite with urea and hydrogen peroxide under evaporation or wet-dry cycling gives adenosine phosphates and phosphites in one pot.
papers.method_data: (abstract only) Aqueous mixtures of phosphite, urea, H2O2 and adenosine under warm evaporating-pool (75 to 78 °C) and wet-dry cycling conditions; products identified by 31P and 1H NMR.
papers.key_results: (abstract only) Adenosine phosphates, adenosine phosphites, adenosyl adenosine phosphate and trace ADP formed. Total adenosine-phosphorus products reached up to 73% in warm evaporating pools and up to 60% under wet-dry cycling, favouring adenosine phosphate.
papers.limits: (abstract only) Product shares by regioisomer and the role of H2O2 supply on early Earth were not visible in what we opened. Hydrogen peroxide as a reagent needs its own plausible source.
papers.ideas_for_us: Chain with Baidya et al. 2026: a crustal phosphite source plus this oxidation-phosphorylation step gives a two-step phosphite route for the pond table (#5). Score whether H2O2 and urea can co-exist with the upstream nucleoside step without purification.

papers.title: Interfacial microenvironments enable abiotic ribonucleoside formation in micro- and nanoscale compartments
papers.authors: Liu Q, Zhao X, Lee JK, Zare RN
papers.question: Can water interfaces inside tiny compartments make ribonucleosides from ribose, phosphoric acid and nucleobases without enzymes or added catalysts?
papers.tried: Gas-water and oil-water interfaces in micro- and nanoscale compartments create local conditions that allow glycosidic bond formation, whatever the compartment type.
papers.method_data: Comparison across gas-oil-water and gas-water micro/nanobubbles, lipid-bilayer vesicles and oil-water emulsions containing D-ribose, phosphoric acid and nucleobases.
papers.key_results: (abstract only, no numbers given) Ribonucleosides, including cytidine, formed in all compartment types without added catalysts. CO2-based micro/nanobubbles supported sustained cytidine accumulation. Yield depended on compartment size, and oil content in bubbles selectively changed inosine formation.
papers.limits: (abstract only) No yields, concentrations or regioisomer and anomer data were visible in what we opened. Starting from free ribose and nucleobases is the step many other routes avoid because it is inefficient in bulk water. Bubble and emulsion settings are hard to map onto a specific early-Earth place.

papers.title: Carbamoyl phosphate-mediated peptide formation in mild prebiotic environment
papers.authors: Zheng X, Chen F, Zhang M, Yu S, Xie S, Zhao Y, Ying J
papers.question: Can amino acids join into peptides in mild water, without drying cycles, if carbamoyl phosphate is the activator?
papers.tried: Carbamoyl phosphate (CAP) plus Mg2+ activates amino acids two ways at once (N-carbamoylation and O-phosphorylation), and CAP itself can form from urea and phosphate.
papers.method_data: Aqueous amino acid plus CAP with metal ions at mild temperature, product detection by LC-MS; screens of metal ion, pH, Mg2+ level and 12 amino acids; a urea plus phosphate system replacing added CAP.
papers.key_results: With Mg2+, alanine gave dialanine at 8.48 µM, a yield of 0.0424% of starting monomer. Only Mg2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+ promoted dipeptide among the ions tested; Ba2+ plus Mn2+ worked together but not alone. Best pH was about 6 and best Mg2+ window 0.25 to 1.0 mM. All 12 amino acids tested gave dipeptides and tripeptides. CAP formed from urea and phosphate, and a urea plus phosphate plus Mg2+ mix gave dipeptides of Ala, Gly, Phe, Arg, Glu and Trp; leaving out any one of the three gave none. CAP beat cyanate alone at making peptides.
papers.limits: Yields are very low (0.0424% for dialanine). CAP was only confirmed qualitatively when made from urea and phosphate. The paper assumes concentrated phosphate and urea in a pond, which runs into the phosphorus problem it acknowledges.
papers.ideas_for_us: Add a CAP peptide step to the pond route (#5) with its measured yield and its three required inputs (urea, phosphate, Mg2+), then test with our compatibility rule whether it can share a pond with a nucleotide step that also uses urea and phosphate (e.g. Gull et al. 2026) without a purification hand-off.

papers.title: Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth
papers.authors: Anslow RJ, McDonald CH, Bonsor A, Rimmer PB, Rae ASP
papers.question: Could comets have delivered hydrogen cyanide (HCN) to early Earth's land at the high concentrations (about 10 mM) that lab prebiotic chemistry uses?
papers.tried: Combine a dynamical model of short-period comet impacts, atmospheric-entry break-up, HCN survival during impact and the amount of exposed land, all set to best-case values.
papers.method_data: 10^5 Monte Carlo realisations of Earth's comet bombardment in 1 Myr steps, with comet sizes, speeds and angles, atmospheric entry modeled with the atmosentry code, and an HCN impact-survival fit from McDonald et al.
papers.key_results: Earth accreted more than 10^5 comets larger than 100 m, but the median number of impacts delivering more than 10 mM HCN onto land was zero; 54% of runs had none. Among runs with at least one success, the most likely time was 4.41 (+0.11/-0.29) Gya, and fewer than 5% of runs had a success later than 4.03 Gya. Comets smaller than about 100 m burst in the air. Ignoring land limits, Mars gets 744 ± 27 successful impacts, Earth 87 ± 9 and Venus 24 ± 5. Total comet mass accreted was (2.63 ± 0.19) x 10^18 kg, consistent with noble-gas limits.
papers.limits: HCN is used as the end-member; other feedstocks are expected to fare worse but were not modeled. The HCN survival model neglects comet strength and porosity. Exposed-land history is uncertain; a faster crust-growth model raises successes only by a factor of 3. Long-period comets are excluded. Dilution after impact would make things worse still.
papers.ideas_for_us: In the pathway map, any step whose feedstock source is 'cometary HCN' should be scored as unavailable on Earth or flagged as a rare event. The open scripts (github.com/richard17a/comet_delivery_hcn) could be rerun with our own pond-volume and dilution assumptions to set a source probability for the cyanosulfidic and pond routes.
papers.changes_plan: If any of our pathway step tables credits comets as an HCN source for the pond or cyanosulfidic route, that source should be removed or marked as a rare early-Hadean event, since median successful deliveries onto land are zero.

papers.title: Gradual Destruction of Refractory Stardust in Alkali Brines on Asteroid Bennu
papers.authors: Haenecour P, Barnes JJ, Bloch E, Smith LR, Hill D, Glavin DP, Dworkin JP, Connolly HC, et al.
papers.question: What happened to presolar stardust grains and isotopically odd organic matter in Bennu's 'mottled' particles, which saw late alkaline brines?
papers.tried: A late, cold, oxidising, alkaline brine slowly dissolved even tough silicon carbide grains while leaving organic matter isotopically intact.
papers.method_data: Isotope imaging of nine mottled Bennu particles from three OSIRIS-REx samples, searching for presolar grains and C and N isotope anomalies, compared with other Bennu lithologies, Ryugu and chondrites.
papers.key_results: No O-rich presolar grains found (upper limit about 1 ppm). 27 C-rich (SiC) grains found, total abundance 8 (+2/-1) ppm, versus about 36 to 55 ppm in hummocky and angular Bennu particles. Best Bulk Bennu estimates: 4 ± 1 ppm O-rich and 41 ± 4 ppm C-rich presolar grains. 537 isotopically anomalous organic regions (δ15N -838 to 2,674‰), abundance 1,886 ± 81 ppm, indistinguishable from other Bennu, Ryugu and chondrite organics. Supernova-type SiC share about 7% versus about 31% in other Bennu particles.
papers.limits: Small sample (nine particles, one excluded). Abundances are not corrected for detection efficiency. Destruction mechanism is inferred, not reproduced experimentally.
papers.ideas_for_us: For #11/#19: Bennu lithologies differ (mottled particles also have reduced amino acid diversity per the paper's citation), so when scoring our sealed Bennu purine:pyrimidine and ammonia predictions we should record which lithology or aggregate each measurement comes from, and treat lithology as a stratum rather than averaging.

papers.title: An interstellar energetic and non-aqueous pathway to peptide formation
papers.authors: Hopkinson AT, Wilson AM, Pitfield J, Traspas Muiña A, Rácz R, Mifsud DV, Herczku P, Lakatos G, et al.
papers.question: Can peptide bonds form in cold interstellar ice without liquid water?
papers.tried: Proton irradiation of solid glycine ice at 20 K, standing in for cosmic rays and stellar winds, joins glycine into peptides and gives off water.
papers.method_data: Normal, D3- and D5-labelled glycine ices irradiated with 10 keV to 1 MeV protons, followed by infrared spectroscopy, temperature-programmed desorption and mass spectrometry of the residue.
papers.key_results: Glycylglycine (the simplest dipeptide) was detected by mass (m/z 133 for normal and D3 glycine, m/z 137 for D5). Amide I, II and III infrared bands appeared in the 1 MeV residue (Amide I at 1665 cm^-1). Water and fully deuterated water formed as by-products, with isotope patterns that depend on which hydrogens were labelled. Products extended to m/z 300, and a mass at m/z 103.05 fits N-formylglycinamide. CO2 formed from glycine decarboxylation and CO from CO2 breakdown.
papers.limits: No yields or conversion fractions were given in the text we read. Starting from pure glycine ice is an idealised case; real ices are mostly water. Glycine itself has not been detected in the interstellar medium. Mass assignments beyond the dipeptide are tentative.
papers.ideas_for_us: Context for the 'from space' feedstock list. If we ever score an ice route that needs peptides, this gives a qualitative 'possible in ice' input with no yield, so it should be scored as unquantified.
papers.source_opened: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.26814v1 (arXiv version; journal record checked via Crossref)

papers.title: Meteor over New York City: Brines in a primitive CM asteroid
papers.authors: Jenniskens P, Zolensky ME, Gordon A, Gordon J, Hankey M, Silber EA, Giannone MR, Han J, et al.
papers.question: Did CM-type carbonaceous asteroids, like CI-type Ryugu and Bennu, host sodium-rich brines, and what organics does a freshly fallen CM meteorite carry?
papers.tried: Analyse the Hillsborough meteorite, a CM fall recovered within minutes indoors in July 2024, so it escaped rain and soil.
papers.method_data: Fireball trajectory from cameras and radar; petrography, isotopes, exposure ages; bulk C, N, S; FT-ICR mass spectrometry of organics; amino acid and carboxylic acid analyses compared with Murchison run in parallel.
papers.key_results: Hillsborough is the 22nd observed CM fall and the 2nd CM1/2. Small C1 (CM1) clasts hold locally more than 5 wt% Na2O versus 0.09 to 0.36 wt% normal for CM, with Na in dolomite cracks, read as late Na-rich brine. Bulk C 1.76 ± 0.05 wt%, N 0.074 ± 0.003 wt%, S 6.13 ± 0.22 wt%. Oxygenated to non-oxygenated compound ratio falls from 6.1 (Murchison) to 1.9 (Hillsborough) to 1.3 (Kolang), read as deoxygenation with alteration. C2 to C5 amino acids span about 44 to 625 nmol/g (Murchison about 121 to 167 nmol/g); extraterrestrial amino acids were 0.56 and 3.75 times Murchison in two fragments; isovaline is racemic. Pre-atmospheric mass 53 ± 6 kg; cosmic-ray exposure age about 0.2 Ma.
papers.limits: Some contamination from the house (nylon, protein amino acids with L excess, siloxanes). The brine link rests on Na in cracks, not on preserved salts. No nucleobase or ammonia data were reported, so it says nothing direct about purine:pyrimidine or ammonia.
papers.ideas_for_us: Relevance to #11/#19 checked: the paper reports no nucleobases and no ammonia, so it cannot score or inform our sealed purine:pyrimidine versus ammonia predictions. Its one useful point for that work is that extraterrestrial amino acid totals differ between two fragments of one stone (0.56 versus 3.75 times Murchison), a reminder that lithology spread inside one sample can be as large as differences between bodies. If we add a CM comparator to the Bennu/Ryugu analysis, Hillsborough is a low-contamination CM reference for amino acids and organics.

papers.title: Protocell formation on micrometeorites
papers.authors: Jesorka A, Pedrueza-Villalmanzo E, Ciftcioglu E, Jedrasik P, Larsen J, Gözen I
papers.question: Do lipids self-assemble into compartments on micrometeorite surfaces, and do they prefer them over terrestrial particles?
papers.tried: Expose cleaned micrometeorites, magnetic sand particles and model micrometeorites to three lipid types and image the films, nanotubes and vesicles.
papers.method_data: Fluorescent lipid suspensions (archaeal ether lipids, E. coli lipids, a reference mixture with plant-derived lipids) on plasma-cleaned particles; confocal imaging; SEM-EDX of particles.
papers.key_results: Lipids spread, form nanotube networks and transform into spherical compartments on micrometeorites. Archaeal lipids formed protocells preferentially on micrometeorites; E. coli lipids preferred sand and model particles; the reference mix showed no strong preference. Mg, Si and Fe make up 89 to 90% of the particles' elements. One surface had over 40 nanotubes per unit area but few compartments.
papers.limits: Modern lipids, not prebiotic amphiphiles; few particles; qualitative surface coverage; particles were solvent- and plasma-cleaned, unlike natural ones.
papers.ideas_for_us: Context only; would matter for a 'from space' delivery-plus-membrane route if we ever add one.

papers.title: Detection of a four-carbon sugar in interstellar space
papers.authors: Jiménez-Serra I, García de la Concepción J, Cuppen HM, Rey-Montejo M, Sanz-Novo M, Rivilla VM, Martín-Pintado J, Megías A, et al.
papers.question: Is there any sugar in interstellar space?
papers.tried: Search a very line-rich Galactic Centre cloud for C3 and C4 sugars using new lab rotational spectra, and test a grain-surface formation route from two C2 molecules.
papers.method_data: Radio line surveys of G+0.693-0.027 with the Yebes 40 m and IRAM 30 m telescopes (more than 91 GHz covered), LTE line fitting, quantum chemical reaction calculations and kinetic Monte Carlo ice models.
papers.key_results: Erythrulose (a chiral C4 ketose) detected with 12 sets of lines (17 transitions); six mostly unblended, chance-alignment probability 0.2%. Column density (8.7 ± 0.8) x 10^13 cm^-2, abundance (6.4 ± 0.6) x 10^-10. C3 sugars glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone not detected (≤4 x 10^-11 and ≤7 x 10^-11), so erythrulose is at least 8 to 17 times more abundant. Glycolaldehyde and ethylene glycol are 1.1 and 2.7 times the erythrulose abundance and are the proposed precursors. Ice models match methanol, glycolaldehyde, ethylene glycol and erythrulose within a factor of 5 but overproduce C3 sugars by about 25 to 70. Erythrulose/water is about 6 x 10^-6; they estimate about (0.5 to 50) x 10^9 kg could have reached early Earth.
papers.limits: Single source; line blending in a crowded spectrum (six lines carry the identification). The delivery estimate assumes meteorite organics keep ISM ratios to water. The model overproduces C3 sugars, so the chemistry is not fully understood. Ribose itself was not detected.
papers.ideas_for_us: Add an 'exogenous erythrulose to threose' input to the ice-RNA and pond step tables as a feedstock option, scored with the paper's delivered-mass range. It is also a check on our Bennu/Ryugu work: if sample papers report C4 sugars, the erythrulose share relative to glycolaldehyde (about 1:1.1 here) is a simple ratio to compare.

papers.title: Reconstructing ancient genomes from gene counts: A robust likelihood framework with sampling bias correction
papers.authors: Csűrös M
papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.question: Can ancestral genomes be reconstructed robustly from gene counts alone, with a correction for how genomes and families were sampled?
papers.tried: A gain-loss-duplication (GLD) likelihood on copy-number profiles is more robust at depth than reconciling thousands of weakly resolved gene trees.
papers.method_data: Birth-death GLD model with sampling-bias correction; simulations of gain-loss-duplication processes (no transfer gene trees, no sequences); reanalysis of published large reconciliations.
papers.key_results: In simulation GLD recovers ancestral content with median TPR 98.6%. The paper says the root genome is the hardest case. It argues the 700-genome study (Moody 2024) shows transfers correlated with family size (R2 = 0.83), giving a LUCA 'with only 45 genes' (SI Fig. S41), and that the 1,007-genome study reduces the LBCA root to 5 genes.
papers.limits: Simulations test only the profile-based GLD model, not ALE or AleRax. The ALE critique is an empirical argument. The '45 genes' probably counts confident families, not summed PPs; the SI was not opened.
papers.ideas_for_us: Our #32 is the missing simulation: run ALE/AleRax-style reconciliation on Zombi genomes and see whether transfers are overcalled and root content shrinks, as Csűrös says. Used as prior art for T9: it names the DPANN completeness confound and says copy numbers cannot separate it ('perfectly absorbed by increased loss'), which is why T9 tests deep branches only.

papers.title: Phylogenetic reconciliation supports a methanogenic ancestor of the Archaea and a derived origin for host-associated lineages
papers.authors: Huang WC, Dombrowski N, Mahendrarajah TA, Wahl N, Stamatakis A, Szöllősi GJ, Williams TA, Spang A
papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.question: Where is the root of the archaeal tree, and what was the last archaeal common ancestor (LACA) like? Does letting duplication, transfer and loss rates vary across the tree change the answer?
papers.tried: Reconciliation models with clade-specific D, T and L rates fit the data better than one global rate set, and remove a 'small genome attraction' artefact that pulls the root toward genome-reduced DPANN symbionts.
papers.method_data: 257 archaeal genomes; 7,059 arCOG-based gene families, 1,000 bootstrap gene trees each, reconciled in AleRax v1.1.1 against 15 candidate rooted species trees. CheckM2 completeness used as fraction missing. Models: global (3 parameters), per-family (21,177), DPANN-specific loss, then clade-wise DTL models with 21, 25, 72 (DTL_br2) and 81 parameters, compared by BIC and AU tests (CONSEL). Ancestral content from the 72-parameter model with origination rates optimised separately for the root, its two children and DPANN (--origination OPTIMISE). Family counts by PP >= 0.5 and >= 0.75; genome size by LOESS of protein number vs genome size in extant genomes, 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Also re-ran Williams et al.'s 60-genome dataset. Outgroup, non-reversible (NONREV) and non-stationary (GFmix) rooting run in parallel.
papers.key_results: Global model favoured a DPANN Cluster 2 root driven by small, biased families. Adding a DPANN loss rate improved fit; DPANN loss 0.40-0.45 vs 0.26-0.27 for other clades. Best robust model (72 parameters) kept only the Euryarchaeota root and the adjacent MHH root (P >= 0.48); the 81-parameter model favoured the Euryarchaeota root (P = 0.99) over MHH (P = 0.024). Re-analysis of the old 60-genome set moved support from DPANN to the Euryarchaeota root (P = 1). Ancestral reconstructions across models correlate at Pearson r > 0.98. Mean verticality 79%; transfers 10.87-11.18 times more frequent than duplications. LACA genome size 1.58 Mb (95% BCI 1.54-1.61) for the Euryarchaeota root and 2.06 Mb (2.01-2.11) for the MHH root; 800-1,219 arCOG families (Euryarchaeota root) and 1,190-1,709 (MHH root). Methyl-coenzyme M reductase subunits at PP 0.39-0.96 (e.g. McrA 0.5/0.58). LACA optimal growth temperature median 78.78 C (74.15-83.52). DPANN ancestor 1.32/1.68 Mb, 546-827/820-1,152 families.
papers.limits: No simulation of ancestral gene-content recovery is reported in the main text or methods (the word 'simulation' does not appear); we did not open the Supplementary Notes, so a check there is still open. No correction for false negatives or false positives at the root: family counts are raw PP thresholds (methods say counts of PP >= 0.5 and >= 0.75; results say 'integrating over the LACA PPs'), and pathway calls use PP >= 0.5. Only archaeal subfamilies are reconciled, so inter-domain transfers are invisible. arCOG annotation covers 47.08-99.8% of genes per genome (median 82.3%), so genome size is extrapolated from annotated families.
papers.ideas_for_us: 1) A second real-data target for #32: the per-family LACA PPs (Supplementary Data 25 and 26) and the AleRax reconciliation outputs on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/18701544) come from the same toolchain we simulate. A calibration learned at LUCA depth could be re-fit at archaeal-root depth and applied to their 7,059 PPs, giving a calibrated LACA count to compare with 800-1,709. 2) Add clade-varying loss rates to the Zombi truth model (e.g. a reduced-genome clade with loss about 1.6x the background, matching 0.40-0.45 vs 0.26-0.27) and test whether a global-rate AleRax fit, as Moody et al. used, biases root PP. 3) Their origination-rate-at-root option is a model choice that directly moves root PP; include it as a factor in the calibration grid. T9 (sealed, 2026-11-24, experiments/t9_dpann_completeness/T9_RESULTS.md): is DPANN's higher loss rate an artefact of incomplete genomes? On internal branches with at least 3 genomes, where one incomplete genome cannot create a loss, the DPANN loss fraction is 1.37 times the other archaea's (1.146 to 1.63); support needed a lower bound above 1.15, so the sealed verdict is inconclusive by a hair. Tip losses do rise with incompleteness, and the DPANN tip excess is explained by it; the deep-branch excess is not.
papers.source_opened: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13473441/fullTextXML (main text and methods; supplementary notes and data not opened)
papers.changes_plan: Does not pre-empt #32: no simulation calibration of deep-node PPs is reported, and LACA content is a raw PP threshold count. The sealed v3 amendment varies rates per family (lognormal, sigma 0.5) but keeps them equal across lineages. Huang et al. show that lineage-specific loss (DPANN 0.40-0.45 vs 0.26-0.27 elsewhere) changes deep-node inference, so a sensitivity arm with clade-varying loss in the Zombi truth model is worth a new sealed amendment. Their LACA per-family PPs (Zenodo 18701544) are a second application target.

papers.title: Models trained with noisy genomes extend bacterial phenotype prediction into deep time
papers.authors: Koldaeva A, Bagrova O, Mitchell JAM, Hugenholtz P, Spang A, Woodcroft B, Williams TA, Szöllősi G
papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.question: Can machine-learning phenotype predictors trained on modern gene-family profiles be applied to noisy reconstructed ancestral genomes, back to the last bacterial common ancestor (LBCA)?
papers.tried: Training on copies of genomes with random gene gains and losses makes predictors robust to the errors in reconstructed ancestral gene content.
papers.method_data: COG copy-number profiles (eggNOG-mapper) for GTDB genomes; five phenotypes (oxygen use, cell envelope, sporulation, optimal growth temperature, GC content) labelled from BacDive, TEMPURA and literature. XGBoost with taxonomy-aware splits (family to domain, 30 splits per level), SHAP and Markov blanket feature analysis. Noise augmentation: false negatives subtract a Poisson-distributed number of counts at rate sFN; false positives add Poisson counts to zero-count families at rate sFP; rates drawn per noisy copy from uniform, exponential or gamma distributions with means lambdaFN and lambdaFP; scheme chosen by area under MCC vs test-noise curves. Applied to ancestral expected copy numbers on a 1,007-bacteria species tree from earlier reconciliation work.
papers.key_results: Oxygen use, cell envelope and mesophile/thermophile classification keep comparable performance with 60-70% of features removed. Noise augmentation improves robustness for oxygen use and cell envelope across all test-noise levels. LBCA predicted to be an anaerobic, non-sporulating, moderately thermophilic diderm with optimal temperature in the 46-75 C range; GC content cannot be inferred at the root. Confidence decays slowly toward the root for broadly encoded traits.
papers.limits: The noise model is generic (independent Poisson false negatives and positives with assumed rate distributions). It is not derived from simulations of reconciliation error, and the paper gives no false-negative or false-positive rate for reconciliation at the LBCA. Authors note it 'cannot fully capture' the phylogenetic covariance of reconstruction error. Supplementary Section 8 (noise parameter details) not opened.
papers.ideas_for_us: Our #32 simulations produce exactly what their augmentation lacks: depth-dependent false-negative and false-positive rates for AleRax root calls, with their correlation structure across families. Report those per-depth error rates in a form (rFN, rFP) they could plug into their augmentation. Data and models: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21018005; code github.com/oist/gene-context.
papers.source_opened: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2026/07/02/2026.06.29.735159.source.xml (v1 JATS full text; supplementary materials not opened)

papers.question: Was LUCA's enzymatic core metabolism complete, and if not, what supplied the missing steps?
papers.tried: Like the ribosome, metabolism was incomplete in LUCA and was finished separately in the bacterial and archaeal stems; native metals (Fe, Co, Ni, Pd) and phosphite at serpentinizing vents stood in for missing enzymes.
papers.method_data: 953 prokaryotic genomes clustered (DIAMOND, MCL; 103,482 clusters with >= 4 sequences); clusters annotated to 424 core metabolic reactions via SwissProt/UniProt, merged by sequence and AlphaFold structure similarity (TM-score >= 0.5). LUCA presence was a phyletic rule, not reconciliation: a cluster traces to LUCA if present in >= 50% of genomes of >= 4 higher taxa in both bacteria and archaea; LBCA or LACA if this holds in only one domain; others manually placed in grey zones. Lab tests of Ni0 and Pd0 catalysed phosphorylation by phosphite.
papers.key_results: 166 core-metabolism enzymes trace to LUCA; 89 arose on the lineage to LBCA and 38 on the lineage to LACA; 37 too sparse to assign. LUCA ribosome had 33 proteins, with 29 and 21 added on the archaeal and bacterial lineages. Nucleotide synthesis enzymatically complete in LUCA; amino acid and cofactor synthesis incomplete. Five reactions catalysed by unrelated enzymes in bacteria and archaea (e.g. alanine dehydrogenase). Ni0 with 200 mM phosphite and 100 mM AMP gave 6.74 uM ADP after 96 h at 50 C.
papers.limits: LUCA calls rely on a presence-in-both-domains rule with no model of transfer or loss, so early inter-domain transfer can create false LUCA calls and deep loss can create false absences. Results depend on clustering thresholds and a 953-genome sample. Phosphite concentrations exceed those measured in serpentinized rocks (authors note this).
papers.ideas_for_us: #32: their rule (>= 50% of genomes in >= 4 higher taxa in each domain) is a pure occupancy classifier. Run it on our simulated genomes as a baseline beside AleRax root PP, to measure its false-positive rate under transfer. #28 and #23: their 166 LUCA enzymes and reaction assignments (repository doi 10.25838/d5p-91) are an independent enzyme-age labelling to test against metabolic strata and Rhea network seeds.
papers.source_opened: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13440417/fullTextXML (abstract, LUCA results, methods for family assignment, phosphite results; supplementary tables not opened)

papers.title: The last bacterial common ancestor encoded the components of a functionally complete flagellum
papers.authors: Selcuk B, Andrianova EP, Beeby M, Kearns DB, Erhardt M, Zhulin IB
papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.question: Did the last bacterial common ancestor have a simple flagellum that was elaborated later, or have deep reconstructions missed divergent homologs?
papers.tried: Sensitive homology searches plus co-presence and gene-tree evidence will find many more ancestral flagellar genes than the 24 previously inferred.
papers.method_data: 80,789 GTDB r214 bacterial proteomes; KOfam/Pfam HMMs and iterative profile searches at relaxed E-values; pairwise co-presence (Jaccard) of 53 flagellar genes; an order-level consensus tree built from 74 flagellar gene trees and rooted between Gracilicutes and Terrabacteria; ancestral presence by broad distribution across both superclades without signs of recent transfer. No probabilistic reconciliation (ALE/AleRax) is used.
papers.key_results: Europe PMC copy: 52 ancestral flagellar proteins (28 more than the earlier 24); 40 genes strongly co-present; most flagellated genomes keep 41-44 ancestral proteins; no extant genome has all 52; core export and motor genes absent from only about 2-5% of genomes. Latest bioRxiv abstract (v2): 49 groups with high-confidence support across three phylogenetic reconstructions plus 1 likely, 50 in total. Several homologs (FliF, FliH, FlrC, MotB) were missed until searches were rerun with alternative queries.
papers.limits: Ancestral presence is judged from distribution on a consensus tree, not a probabilistic model, so transfer between superclades could inflate the count. Numbers differ between versions (52 vs 50). The v2 methods were not read.
papers.ideas_for_us: Evidence on the false-negative side for #32 that sits upstream of reconciliation: divergent homologs are missed or split into separate families, so a family can look younger than it is. Add a homology-detection failure step (splitting a family into lineage-specific clusters at high divergence) to the simulated pipeline and measure how much it lowers root PP. flagelladb.org gives per-genome presence data for a check against Moody's flagellar families.
papers.source_opened: Europe PMC preprint full text PPR1251502 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PPR1251502/fullTextXML, preprint dated 2026-06-12); v2 abstract (2026-11-13) via api.biorxiv.org. v2 full text not opened (bioRxiv rate limit).

papers.title: Tryptophan became part of the universal genetic code post-LUCA
papers.authors: Wehbi S, Ly-Trong N, Wheeler A, Minh BQ, Lauretta D, Masel J
papers.topic: LUCA and the tree of life
papers.question: Was tryptophan already in the genetic code of LUCA, judged by when tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase (WRS) split from tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (YRS)?
papers.tried: If the WRS/YRS tree roots between bacterial and archaeal YRS, WRS arose after LUCA inside Archaea and spread to Bacteria by transfer.
papers.method_data: PF00579 catalytic domain sequences; removal of ancient archaeal-bacterial recombinant YRS sequences; amino acid plus 3Di structural alphabet partitions; new archaea-trained time non-reversible model NQ.arch alongside NQ.bac; 1,000 bootstrap trees reconciled with the Web of Life species tree in AleRax; rooting by CRS outgroup, midpoint, MAD and NQ rootstrap. Ancestral amino acid frequencies in pre-LACA (63 Pfams), pre-LBCA (575) and LUCA clans by IQ-TREE ancestral reconstruction with gaps.
papers.key_results: After removing recombinant sequences all rooting methods place the root between bacterial and archaeal YRS. NQ root has 100% rootstrap under both bacterial and archaeal models. Reconstructed W frequency: pre-LBCA 0.014 +/- 0.0008, pre-LACA 0.008 +/- 0.002, LUCA 0.010 +/- 0.0006. Bacterial YRS ancestor has four W sites at > 99% probability. Two essential W-synthesis domains (PF00218, PF00425) are post-LUCA; the authors suggest an earlier 50% LUCA presence for trpE in Moody et al. 2024 may reflect its other domain (PF04715), which does trace to LUCA.
papers.limits: Single gene family; conclusions depend on correctly identifying and removing recombinant sequences. W-usage comparisons rely on ancestral reconstructions at low-confidence sites (about 35% of pre-LACA W from sites < 70% confidence).
papers.ideas_for_us: Two failure modes for #32's truth model: (1) a gene transferred between the bacterial and archaeal stems just after LUCA yields a gene tree that looks like a LUCA split; Zombi runs should include stem-to-stem transfers and score how often AleRax calls those LUCA. (2) Multi-domain families can inherit a LUCA PP from one domain; flag Moody families whose KO maps to fused domains before applying the calibration. Code and data: github.com/sawsanwehbi/Ancient-Tryptophan-Tyrosine-usage.

papers.title: A Hadean timeline for the emergence of the RNA World
papers.authors: Abramov O, Medvegy A, Kremer B, Mojzsis SJ
papers.question: When did impact bombardment of the Hadean crust ease enough for an RNA World to persist?
papers.tried: A 3-D thermal model of late accretion, checked against Jack Hills zircon ages, can date when near-surface volumes stayed cool enough for biomolecules.
papers.method_data: Global 3-D bombardment thermal model with Brasser, Neukum and Werner chronologies; delivered masses 0.13-0.57 wt% of Earth; zircon Pb-loss age-resetting compared with Jack Hills ages; biocompatible volumes (< 110 C, 20-50 C), never-sterilized volumes, hydrothermal zones (> 140 C/km, < 110 C) and cluster counts in the upper 300 m, scaled to 5% land exposure.
papers.key_results: Frequent global sterilization until about 4.4 Ga. Near-surface biocompatible volume rises to > 90% by 4.3 Ga. Hydrothermal volumes peak about 4.4 Ga; hydrothermal clusters peak at 4.3 Ga. Never-sterilized volume becomes non-zero only after about 4.4 Ga. Ocean-vaporizing impacts fewer than 1 per 10 Myr after 4.4 Ga. 'Sweet spot' about 4.33 Ga, about 130 Myr before a LUCA at about 4.2 Ga (window 4.09-4.33). With 0.13 wt% the sweet spot moves about 70 Myr earlier, to about 4.4 Ga.
papers.limits: Delivered mass is a critical and uncertain parameter (authors say so). Thermal stability thresholds stand in for chemistry. The LUCA window is taken from earlier clock studies, not tested.
papers.ideas_for_us: Context for the time budget between habitability and LUCA. If #32 shrinks LUCA's gene count, the 'compressed time' argument changes; this paper gives the geophysical side of that budget.

papers.title: Molecular assembly as a universal biosignature measurable by mass spectrometry
papers.authors: Rutter LA, Sharma A, Seet I, Obeh Alobo D, Goto A, Cronin L
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 123(33):e2619198123
papers.question: Can the molecular assembly index (MA) of a molecule be predicted from single-stage mass spectra (MS1), as flown on Titan and Europa missions, and is MA a better life-detection score than the Bertz and Bottcher complexity scores?
papers.tried: Argue that MA is more interpretable than Bertz and Bottcher, then train a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost) to predict a molecule's MA from its MS1 spectrum.
papers.method_data: MA computed with assemblyCPP v5 for all NIST SRD 69 molecules with EI MS1 spectra (n = 32,603), plus COCONUT 2.0 (n = 526,968) and PubChem (n = 99,129,693) for scaling comparisons. XGBoost trained on 70% and tested on 30% (stratified by MA), loss = relative MSE. Baselines: linear, log, power-law and polynomial fits on molecular weight, bond count, max peak and peak count. External test on MassBank EI-B MS1. Simulated ESI MS2 spectra from CFM-ID 4 at 10, 20 and 40 eV.
papers.key_results: Power-law scaling with bond count: MA beta = 0.74 (R2 0.74) on NIST, 0.68 (0.64) on COCONUT 2.0, 0.74 (0.72) on PubChem; Bertz 1.46/1.34/1.49; Bottcher 0.96/1.09/1.00. XGBoost cut relative MSE from 0.12 (best baseline) to 0.04 on NIST; 0.07 on MassBank versus 0.12 for the best power law on molecular weight. Simulated spectra gave 0.033, 0.031 and 0.031 (10, 20, 40 eV), 0.035 for mixed-energy training and 0.029 for concatenated energies; a 40 eV model tested on 10 eV data rose from 0.031 to 0.060. Low-MA molecules are overpredicted and high-MA molecules underpredicted. Maximum MA in the NIST set is 24. At matched bond count, PubChem molecules have higher MA than COCONUT 2.0 natural products; the strict bound MA = NB - 1 holds up to NB = 14 in COCONUT and NB = 24 in PubChem. Mapping MA thresholds of 15 to 20 onto Bertz or Bottcher gives false positive rates of 0.17 to 0.32.
papers.limits: No biotic versus abiotic samples were measured; the paper predicts MA, it does not test whether MA separates life from non-life. The comparison against molecular weight is only for predicting MA, not for classifying origin. Their own size-matched database comparison goes the 'wrong' way (synthetic-heavy PubChem has higher MA than natural products at the same bond count), which they reinterpret as possible technosignatures. The life threshold of about 15 is taken from Marshall et al. 2021, not retested. Per-molecule MA needs chromatographic separation first.
papers.ideas_for_us: For #22: their Zenodo deposit (10.5281/zenodo.20586263) gives MA for NIST, and the paper reports MA by bond count for COCONUT vs PubChem; we can rerun our size-matched test on it and check whether natural products sit below PubChem at every bond count, as their Fig. 5C says. For #7: their MS1 to MA model error versus a molecular-weight power law (0.04 vs 0.12) is a template for our 'does AI beat size' test; we can ask the same question for classification instead of regression. Code: github.com/croningp/assemblycpp-v5.
papers.source_opened: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13486590/ (PMC full text; pnas.org returned a bot challenge)

papers.title: The diverse effects of side reactions on the persistence of autocatalytic cycles
papers.authors: Peng Z, Spencer E, Baum D
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
papers.question: Do side reactions necessarily kill autocatalytic cycles without specialized catalysts, as critics of metabolism-first theories argue?
papers.tried: Treat all reactions as reversible in an open, fed reactor; side products then act as a reservoir that can regenerate the autocatalyst.
papers.method_data: Algebraic steady-state analysis of A + F <-> 2A with side reaction A <-> B in a CSTR (rates k1 to k4, dilution kd, food f), compared with the same cycle without a side reaction; Gillespie stochastic simulations for low copy numbers; algebra for a two-reaction cycle with three side reactions. papers.key_results: With an irreversible side reaction the autocatalyst persists only if k1 > k3 + kd/f, and the side reaction always lowers the steady-state autocatalyst level. A cycle can persist even when the autocatalytic step is thermodynamically disfavored (k2 > k1).
papers.limits: Very small idealized networks, well-mixed, mass action plus small stochastic cases; no real chemistry. 'Beneficial' is measured by total direct plus indirect autocatalyst, which the authors note may not map linearly onto extinction risk.
papers.ideas_for_us: For #6/#8/#23: our RAF null tests ignore reversibility and side products. We could add reversible side reactions to the planted-core recovery (#8) and see whether persistence of the planted core under simulation separates it from null RAFs better than graph-only detection does. papers.ideas_for_us: Done as T1 (experiments/t1_vent_exergonic/T1_RESULTS.md). The general lesson: a share of exergonic reactions needs a reversed and a matched-null control before it says anything about a setting.

papers.title: A thermodynamic basis for prebiotic amino acid synthesis and the nature of the first genetic code
papers.authors: Higgs PG, Pudritz RE
papers.question: Do the amino acids that are easiest to make abiotically match the ones that entered the genetic code first?
papers.tried: Combine amino-acid frequencies from discharge experiments, hydrothermal-vent simulations and meteorites into one ranking, then compare it with free energies of formation and with a consensus code order.
papers.method_data: Table 1 of 12 abiotic sources (meteorites, spark discharge and others); Table 2 with observed rank, code rank (Trifonov 2004), relative concentration, free energy of formation (Amend and Shock 1998), ATP cost and molecular weight.

Across discharge, vent and meteorite sources these ten early amino acids fall in one consistent order of decreasing abundance, which thermodynamics predicts. The authors argue the first proteins reflected these abundances and the other ten were added later, stepwise.
papers.limits: The consensus order they compare with has since been revised (Wehbi 2024). Amino acids never observed share one bottom rank. Abundance and molecular weight are strongly linked, which our T2 controls for.
papers.ideas_for_us: Prior art behind T2. Our partial correlation, controlling for molecular weight, finds no abundance effect in the returned asteroid samples; Murchison's raw association falls from 0.46 to 0.25 once weight is controlled.

papers.title: Theoretical basis for stabilizing messenger RNA through secondary structure design
papers.authors: Wayment-Steele HK, Kim DS, Choe CA, et al.
papers.question: How fast does an RNA strand break by hydrolysis, and how much does folding protect it?
papers.tried: Write down one equation for the break rate of each RNA link, built from the Li and Breaker 1999 measurements, and use it to design mRNA that lasts longer in storage.
papers.method_data: Methods section 'Quantitative model for RNA hydrolysis'. The rate per link depends on pH, temperature, potassium and magnesium, from a reference point of pH 6, 23 C and 3.17 M potassium. It was fitted with 5 to 10 mM magnesium. Table 1 prints worked rates for storage conditions.
papers.key_results: Gives the rate law that T3 coded: a base rate of 1.3e-9 per minute per link at pH 6 and 23 C, about tenfold faster per pH unit and about tenfold faster per 14 C. They multiply by length and by the unpaired fraction (0.4) to get a rate per molecule.
papers.limits: The equation prints 3.16 M in one place and 3.17 M in the sentence after, and the paper does not say why. Their own text says the fit used 5 to 10 mM magnesium and that with no magnesium the last two terms are dropped. Our code matched 5 of the 6 rates in their Table 1 within 1%; the sixth (in vitro transcription, 37 C, pH 7.6, 14 mM Mg) came out 2.2 times lower than printed and we could not find the cause.
papers.ideas_for_us: T3 (RNA persistence per origin setting; not decidable, see T3_STATUS.md). This is the second open copy of the Li and Breaker law, so T3 could use it without the paywalled original. It also gave T3 a published table to test the code against.
papers.source_opened: full text (PMC8499941, CC BY 4.0); metadata from PRIOR_ART

papers.title: Prebiotic gas flow environment enables isothermal nucleic acid replication
papers.authors: Schwintek P, et al.
papers.question: Can a heated pore with gas flowing through it copy nucleic acids at one steady temperature, and do the copies outlast the breakage?

papers.method_data: Appendix 8, equation 19 repeats the Li and Breaker law (magnesium, salt, pH, temperature, length). It uses sodium in the experiment but assumes the potassium correction would be similar. Worked example for a 24-mer at 45 C, pH 7, 50 to 200 micromolar magnesium.
papers.key_results: For a 24-mer at 45 C they print 8.917e-6 per minute (200 micromolar Mg) and 3.231e-5 per minute (1 mM Mg), a break time near 2,000 hours. They state that copying with plausible machinery 'out-competes' hydrolysis in their settings. They quote a nonenzymatic copy rate of 1 per hour (from Walton 2019) and a ribozyme rate of 72 per hour.
papers.limits: The paper does not print the potassium value it used. Setting potassium to 1 mM reproduces both printed numbers exactly in our check, but that is our back-calculation, not something the paper states. It covers one lab condition.
papers.ideas_for_us: T3 (not decidable, see T3_STATUS.md). This is the copy-time versus break-time comparison that T3 wanted to run across many natural settings, done for a single lab setting. It was the second open source for the rate law and a check on our code.

papers.authors: Cohen ZR, Ding D, Zhou L, DasGupta S, Haas S, Sinclair KP, Todd ZR, Black RA, Szostak JW, Catling DC

A ligase ribozyme worked after the pH was lowered from about 10 to 9 (60% in 20 h at 1.2 mM Mg in lab buffer; 32% and 11% in lake water). Primers were not seen to break after 72 hours in lake water. Vesicles of 1:1 decanoic acid and decanol kept their dye in lake water, but only if formed first in dilute water.

T4 extends this two-lake joint test to a database of natural waters, and finds hot-spring and vent chemistry almost never meets both windows. T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): the soda-lake route (carbonate removes Ca while about 1 mM Mg stays) that T7 tests on Yellowstone spring water. papers.title: Darwinian properties and their trade-offs in autocatalytic RNA reaction networks
papers.authors: Ameta S, Arsène S, Foulon S, Saudemont B, Clifton BE, Griffiths AD, Nghe P
papers.question: Do networks of self-assembling Azoarcus ribozyme fragments show heritable, selectable properties, and do growth and variability trade off?

papers.title: A Comprehensive Methodology for Monitoring Evaporitic Mineral Precipitation and Hydrochemical Evolution of Saline Lakes: The Case of Lake Magadi Soda Brine (East African Rift Valley, Kenya)
papers.authors: Getenet M, García-Ruiz JM, Otálora F, Emmerling F, Al-Sabbagh D, Verdugo-Escamilla C
papers.question: In what order do minerals precipitate as Lake Magadi soda brine evaporates, and how does the brine chemistry change along the way?
papers.tried: Evaporate Lake Magadi brine in acoustically levitated droplets watched by video microscopy and synchrotron X-ray diffraction, characterise the minerals ex situ, and compare with a thermodynamic evaporation model.
papers.method_data: In situ video microscopy and synchrotron XRD of levitated droplets; ex situ Raman, XRD and SEM; PHREEQC 3.4 with the Pitzer database for speciation, evaporation and precipitation, starting from a measured brine (Table 1).
papers.key_results: Model path by concentration factor (CF): amorphous silica supersaturates at CF 3; nahcolite precipitates between CF 6.2 and 16.4; calcite starts dissolving and gaylussite forms at CF 8.6 until 11.5, then pirssonite; trona first at CF 9.7; halite from CF 32. pH falls slightly from 9.8 to 9.4 up to CF 6.4. Alkaline-earth carbonates and fluorite are predicted first, then siliceous sediments; halite/villiaumite, thermonatrite and sylvite follow trona. The experiments reproduce the mineral assemblages seen in the lake.
papers.limits: One brine from one lake. The authors note that predicted and measured sulfate and phosphate disagree, which they read as biological cycling. Sylvite and glaserite are predicted near complete dryness but not reported in the basin.
papers.ideas_for_us: T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): the gate. T7 reran this published PHREEQC + Pitzer path from the Table 1 brine and had to match it within a factor of 1.3: nahcolite onset CF 6.25 (published 6.2), trona 9.70 (9.7), halite 28.0 (32), amorphous silica 3.08 (3.0), and the small pH drop; 5 of 5 checks passed.

papers.title: Halite crystallization at Sfax solar salterns, Tunisia, driven by brine geochemistry and biogeochemical interactions
papers.authors: Gharsalli N, Mhiri N, Yaich C, Karray F
papers.question: How do brine geochemistry and halophilic microbes shape halite crystallisation along the evaporation gradient of a seawater-fed saltern?
papers.tried: Analyse 26 brines along the Sfax saltern gradient, isolate halophilic archaea from three basins, and run crystallisation experiments with increasing biomass inoculum against abiotic controls.
papers.method_data: Major-ion geochemistry of 26 brine samples (mean salinity about 28-570 g/L); enrichment cultures from surface and bottom brines; controlled halite crystallisation with 25-75% inoculum.
papers.key_results: The brines follow a marine evaporation sequence. Calcium rises linearly with the potassium-based concentration factor (FC) to about 5 times seawater, then falls sharply as gypsum precipitation intensifies (FC 5-8). Halite starts forming around FC 11. Three Halorubrum species were isolated from cultures tolerating up to 280 g/L; surface-brine cultures gave 5.550 +/- 0.127 g of halite-dominated precipitate after 10 days at 25% inoculum.
papers.limits: One saltern, a field sequence rather than a controlled evaporation. The concentration factor is based on potassium. Most of the paper is about microbes and crystal form, not the ion path.
papers.ideas_for_us: T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): the halite bound in the seawater gate. T7's check G3 (halite onset CF between 9.5 and 13.0) brackets this field value; T7 got 11.10.

papers.title: A carbonate-rich lake solution to the phosphate problem of the origin of life
papers.authors: Toner JD, Catling DC
papers.question: Can carbonate-rich lakes hold the high phosphate levels that prebiotic syntheses use, when most natural waters lose phosphate to apatite?
papers.tried: Model evaporation and steady-state inflow of carbonate-rich waters with PHREEQC, tracking how calcium is taken up in carbonates instead of apatite.
papers.method_data: PHREEQC with the phreeqc.dat database; evaporation and steady-state lake models; comparison with measured phosphate in carbonate-rich lakes (Fig. 1).
papers.key_results: Modern carbonate-rich lakes could hold up to about 0.1 molal phosphate at steady state with evaporation and inflow, because calcium is locked in carbonates. Evaporation without inflow can reach more than 1 molal. On evaporation, Ca and Mg precipitate as carbonates and silicates and the brine becomes Na-HCO3-CO3 rich. Under early CO2-rich air the brines would be buffered to pH 6.5-9.
papers.limits: About phosphate, not membranes or RNA. The authors name the problem that high salt destabilises lipid vesicles and inhibits RNA oligomerisation, and call it potentially resolvable without testing it.
papers.ideas_for_us: T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): the mechanism T7 asks about (carbonate strips Ca on evaporation). T7 applies it to Yellowstone spring waters and scores the path against the vesicle and RNA windows, which this paper does not do.

papers.title: Biogeochemical explanations for the world's most phosphate-rich lake, an origin-of-life analog
papers.authors: Haas S, Sinclair KP, Catling DC
papers.question: Why does Last Chance Lake hold so much dissolved phosphate?
papers.tried: Test explanations by studying phosphorus and nitrogen cycling in Last Chance Lake and Goodenough Lake, Canada: sediment mineralogy, phosphorus sinks and N2-fixation rates.
papers.method_data: Field sampling of water and sediment in two soda lakes; sediment calcium mineralogy; N2-fixation measurements.
papers.key_results: No geochemical phosphorus precipitation was found; sedimentary calcium is in dolomite rather than apatite; N2 fixation, probably suppressed by high salinity, is too low to create much biological phosphate demand. Last Chance Lake reaches 37 mM phosphate, the highest known natural level. Plagioclase weathering gives Na-HCO3-CO3 water from which calcite precipitates early and completely on evaporation.
papers.limits: Two modern lakes on basalt. About phosphate, not membranes or RNA copying.
papers.ideas_for_us: T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): prior art for calcite removing Ca early on evaporation of basalt-derived water. T7 tests whether the same route works for hot-spring water and still leaves the vesicle window open.

papers.title: Groundwater-Driven Evolution of Prebiotic Alkaline Lake Environments
papers.authors: Tutolo BM, Perrin R, Lauer R, Bossaer S, Tosca NJ, Hutchings A, Sevgen S, Nightingale M, Ilg D, Mott EB, Wilson T
papers.question: How do physical processes (evaporation, groundwater inflow, mixing) drive the chemistry of prebiotic alkaline lakes?
papers.tried: Study the neighbouring Last Chance and Goodenough Lakes, British Columbia, with near-surface geophysics, aqueous geochemistry and hydrogeologic modelling.
papers.method_data: Near-surface geophysics, water chemistry and hydrogeologic models of two small alkaline lakes with contrasting evaporation.
papers.key_results: Extreme phosphate enrichment needs a lake that is geomorphologically prone to evaporation. The density contrast between evaporated brines and inflowing groundwater drives Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities and vigorous surface-subsurface mixing, which the authors offer as a way to reconcile conflicting needs of UV light, salinity, metals and pH.
papers.limits: Two lakes. The authors note that the evaporation that raises phosphate also raises other solutes and may inhibit some lipid membranes, but they do not test a vesicle or RNA window.
papers.ideas_for_us: T7 (inconclusive, see experiments/t7_evaporation_window/T7_RESULTS.md): prior art. It raises the salt-versus-membrane conflict for evaporating lakes; T7 tests that conflict along modelled paths for hot-spring water.

papers.title: Large closed-basin lakes sustainably supplied phosphate during the origins of life
papers.authors: Walton CR, Hao J, Schönbächler M, Shorttle O
papers.question: Could closed-basin lakes keep high phosphate at steady state while phosphate is being used up?
papers.tried: Build a steady-state phosphate budget for closed-basin lakes, with Mono Lake, California, as the case study, and compare lake classes by size and inflow.
papers.method_data: Steady-state P budget with inflow, recycling and abiotic sinks; modern lake data.
papers.key_results: Mono Lake keeps just below 1 mM dissolved phosphate through the year, well mixed, while supporting productivity of about 100 mM C per m2 per day. Smaller closed basins can swing from about 1 mM to orders of magnitude lower with the seasons. When abiotic sinks start depends largely on how carbonate-rich and divalent-cation-poor the lake is.
papers.limits: A phosphate budget only; no ion-window or membrane modelling.

papers.authors: Mulkidjanian AY, Dibrova DV, Bychkov AY

papers.title: RNA sequence to structure analysis from comprehensive pairwise mutagenesis of multiple self-cleaving ribozymes
papers.authors: Roberts JM, Beck JD, Pollock TB, Bendixsen DP, Hayden EJ
papers.question: Do complete single- and double-mutant activity maps of self-cleaving ribozymes carry their structure, including tertiary contacts?
papers.tried: Measure the cleavage of every single and double mutant of five ribozymes (CPEB3, HDV, hammerhead, hairpin, twister) by sequencing, and read structure from epistasis heat maps.
papers.method_data: Co-transcriptional self-cleavage, fraction cleaved from read counts, three replicates; epistasis as log(RA_ij / (RA_i RA_j)). Data and code at GitLab, archived at swh:1:rev:7be31e58784ab6ffe5f15790ebbda98279af84d2 (also holds a hatchet ribozyme not in the paper).
papers.key_results: Base-paired regions show anti-diagonal lines of strong positive epistasis, and disrupting fewer base pairs gives higher epistasis. Hairpin loops A and B show positive epistasis; the hammerhead loop-loop contact does not ('double mutants do not show positive epistasis').
papers.limits: Tertiary contacts are shown by heat maps and by region, with no score of contacts against non-contact pairs matched on separation and single-mutant effects. The paper says CPEB3 has no crystal structure; one exists (PDB 7QR3, 2022).
papers.ideas_for_us: T11 (sealed, 2026-11-24, experiments/t11_ribozyme_epistasis/T11_RESULTS.md): we scored contacts against matched non-contacts with a noise-scaled epistasis z. Base pairs: pooled Δ 0.44 (0.33-0.50), so the method works. Tertiary contacts: Δ 0.11 (-0.02 to 0.23), inconclusive. The faint, consistent signal (about AUC 0.6 in every ribozyme with harmful singles) is real-looking but not established. This gives our QT45 study (#30) its missing positive control.

papers.authors: Zhang Z, Xiong P, Zhang T, Wang J, Zhan J, Zhou Y
papers.question: Can base pairs, including pseudoknots and lone pairs, be inferred from single-to-triple mutant fitness data?
papers.tried: Fit a support-vector model of double-mutant activity from the two singles, and call base pairs from the deviations.

Base pairs from mutant scans are established, so T11 uses them only as a positive control and tests non-base-pair contacts. Their global fit of doubles from singles is the same idea as our isotonic fit.

papers.authors: Andreasson JOL, Savinov A, Block SM, Greenleaf WJ
papers.question: Which double mutants of the glmS ribozyme rescue the activity of a harmful single mutant, and what does that say about its structure?

papers.title: Experimental exploration of a ribozyme neutral network using evolutionary algorithm and deep learning
papers.authors: Rotrattanadumrong R, Yokobayashi Y

papers.tried: Explore a ligase ribozyme's sequence space for eight generations with a genetic algorithm and an MLP trained on measured activities, plus a complete 2^16 library between two genotypes.

papers.title: What time is it in Assembly Space? Cronin and Walker's "The Physics of Causation" fails elementary dimensional analysis (Comment on arXiv:2601.00515)
papers.authors: Moriarty P
papers.question: Does assembly theory's link between the assembly index and clock time hold up dimensionally?
papers.tried: Dimensional analysis of the equations in Cronin and Walker's 'The Physics of Causation' (arXiv:2601.00515v3) that tie assembly steps to continuous time.
papers.method_data: Theoretical comment; no data. Checks the dimensions of v(t)=(1+h)^t, the identity Δt=h=1/P and a=t·Δt, and of the Ω prefactor in their 'Assembly' A.
papers.key_results: No assignment of dimensions to h satisfies their three equations and their definitions. If t is a dimensionless count of steps, the e^a weighting reduces to Bernoulli's compound-interest limit with an implicit rate of 1 per step. The new prefactor Ω, 'measured in kJ mol−1' and set to 1, gives 'total causation' the units of a molar energy, yet it is plotted against an entropy. With no rates, the 'finite time' line between spontaneous and selected objects is not testable.
papers.limits: A short critique of one essay. It does not test the assembly index as a biosignature, and it sets aside the compression critiques (Abrahão, Ozelim et al.).
papers.ideas_for_us: Our tasks #7 and #22 treat the assembly index only as a measured number, not as time or causation, so nothing changes there. It adds one more reason to keep a kinetic null: any 'selection threshold' we test should be run against a rate-based model in which high-index molecules form through low barriers.
